Systemic and tropical risk factors: Recent delivery (peripartum cardiomyopathy, typically within 5 months postpartum); heavy alcohol intake; chemotherapy exposure (e.g., doxorubicin).
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) presenting with acute decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
Cardiogenic: Primary pump failure — Rheumatic heart disease, acute coronary syndromes, endomyocardial fibrosis, peripartum cardiomyopathy
Peripartum cardiomyopathy → last month of pregnancy or 5 months postpartum

faq.a: Yes; the mode of delivery does not affect risk, but surgical stress may unmask early dysfunction.
faq.q: Can PPCM occur after a caesarean section?

faq.a: Breastfeeding is generally safe; bromocriptine, if used, requires stopping lactation.
Patients whose LVEF returns >50% within 6 months have a good long‑term outlook, though close follow‑up remains needed.
faq.q: What is the prognosis if LVEF recovers?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman 3 weeks postpartum presents with dyspnoea and leg swelling. Which bedside finding most strongly supports PPCM over preeclampsia‑related pulmonary oedema? — Presence of a reduced LVEF on bedside echo.
You have only a portable ultrasound but no formal echo. How do you proceed to confirm PPCM? — Perform focused cardiac US to assess LV size and contractility; arrange formal echo when feasible.
Why are ACE‑inhibitors contraindicated in this patient’s current pregnancy trimester? — They cause fetal renal dysplasia and skull ossification defects; wait until after delivery.
A patient with PPCM has an LVEF of 28% and a mobile LV thrombus on echo. What is the next step? — Initiate therapeutic low‑molecular‑weight heparin and consider warfarin once stable.
Which tropical infection most commonly worsens PPCM outcomes in East Africa? — HIV infection, due to immune activation and cardiomyopathy synergy.

How would you differentiate endomyocardial fibrosis from PPCM on echo? — Endomyocardial fibrosis shows apical obliteration and restrictive filling; PPCM shows global LV dilation with reduced systolic function.
What is the rationale for using beta‑blockers in PPCM despite low blood pressure? — They improve ventricular remodeling and reduce mortality; start at low dose and titrate carefully.

A woman with recovered LVEF wishes another pregnancy. What counseling do you give? — Advise a pre‑conception cardiac assessment; if LVEF >55% and asymptomatic, pregnancy may be considered with close monitoring.
ai.title: Peripartum Cardiomyopathy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic left‑ventricular systolic dysfunction occurring in the last month of pregnancy or within five months postpartum, without prior heart disease. Diagnosis relies on clinical heart‑failure signs, echocardiography, and exclusion of other causes.

b: Onset: last month of pregnancy to 5 months postpartum
LVEF <45% on echo
No prior structural heart disease
sections.p: PPCM is defined by new‑onset heart failure with left‑ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <45% occurring in the last trimester or within five months after delivery, after excluding other cardiac diseases.

t.b: Confirms reduced LVEF and rules out valvular lesions; a normal echo would argue against PPCM
Shows pulmonary congestion or cardiomegaly; a normal film does not exclude early disease
Elevated levels support heart‑failure diagnosis; very low levels suggest alternative causes

b: Stage A: risk factors, no symptoms
Stage B: structural disease, no symptoms
Stage C: symptoms, LVEF 30‑44% (moderate)
Stage D: refractory symptoms, LVEF <30% (severe)
sections.p: The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) heart‑failure classification (A‑D) is used; additionally, the NYHA functional class and LVEF thresholds guide prognosis.

b: Late‑pregnancy hormonal shift (prolactin cleavage)
Malnutrition, micronutrient deficiency
Infections common in tropics: HIV, malaria, TB, hepatitis B
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (preeclampsia, eclampsia)
Use of traditional herbal remedies with cardiotoxic compounds
sections.p: PPCM is idiopathic but several precipitating factors are recognised, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Dyspnoea at rest or on exertion
Orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
Peripheral oedema, raised jugular venous pressure
Chest discomfort, palpitations
Reduced urine output
sections.p: Patients present with acute decompensated heart failure, often within weeks of delivery, but may have subtle dyspnoea earlier.

b: Echocardiography – essential for LVEF and wall motion
ECG – may show sinus tachycardia, nonspecific ST changes
Basic labs – CBC, renal function, electrolytes, HIV screen
sections.p: Focus on confirming systolic dysfunction, assessing severity, and excluding mimics; adapt when equipment is limited.

t.b: Detects gross LV dilation and reduced contractility; if inconclusive, arrange formal echo when possible
Identify hypokalaemia or hyponatraemia that worsen HF; replace as needed
Positive result may influence prognosis and antiretroviral choice

b: Persistent hypotension (systolic <90 mmHg)
Pulmonary oedema unresponsive to diuretics
Cardiogenic shock
Thrombo‑embolic events (LV thrombus, pulmonary embolism)
Arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation)
sections.p: Rapid deterioration can lead to life‑threatening complications; early recognition is vital.

b: Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) – reduce preload, monitor electrolytes
Beta‑blockers (e.g., carvedilol) – improve remodeling, start low and titrate
ACE‑inhibitors/ARBs – only after delivery; avoid in pregnancy
Bromocriptine (dopamine‑D2 agonist) – experimental, used where prolactin‑mediated injury suspected, watch for thrombosis
Anticoagulation if LVEF <35% or LV thrombus detected – low‑molecular‑weight heparin preferred
sections.p: Treat heart failure while protecting the fetus/infant; avoid drugs harmful in lactation and consider local drug availability.

b: Repeat echo at 3‑6 months, then yearly if LVEF improves
Advise against further pregnancy if LVEF remains <50% or symptomatic
Optimize blood pressure and treat anemia, HIV, or other infections promptly
Educate on low‑salt diet, fluid restriction, and medication adherence
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring of cardiac function and counselling on future pregnancies are essential.

b: Acute rheumatic fever with myocarditis
Endomyocardial fibrosis (common in tropical regions)
Severe preeclampsia‑related pulmonary oedema
Ischaemic cardiomyopathy from coronary artery disease
sections.p: Several conditions mimic PPCM, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Chest X‑ray may be normal in early LV dysfunction
BNP can be modestly raised in pregnancy, masking heart‑failure severity
ECG often nonspecific; a normal ECG does not exclude PPCM
sections.p: Certain investigations may appear normal early, leading to delayed diagnosis.
